```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(sf)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(arrow)
library(leaflet)
library(here)

# source(here("02_code/functions/theme_swank.R"))     # theme_swank(), swank_palette
# source(here("02_code/functions/read_odt.R"))         # read_odt(), keep_oh_counties()
# source(here("02_code/functions/viz_helpers.R"))      # theme_swank_map(), maps, scales
# source(here("02_code/functions/incidence.R"))        # property_tax_incidence(), wtd_quantile_bins()

fig_dir <- here("output/figures")

# Geographies, reprojected to EPSG:3735 (area-correct Ohio). County cb file is
# shoreline-clipped, so Lake Erie is not a polygon.
wi_shp  <- st_read("C:/Users/aryan/OneDrive - American Bankers Association/Documents/GitHub/Wisconsin_Tax/data/shapefiles/CTV_Jan_2026_-4910906020273727621/CTV_Jan_2026.shp")

wi_city <- wi_shp %>% filter(CTV == "C") %>% st_transform(3735)
wi_village <- wi_shp %>% filter(CTV == "V") %>% st_transform(3735)
wi_township <- wi_shp %>% filter(CTV == "T") %>% st_transform(3735)
wi_county <- st_read("C:/Users/aryan/OneDrive - American Bankers Association/Documents/GitHub/Wisconsin_Tax/data/shapefiles/cb_2018_us_county_500k/cb_2018_us_county_500k.shp") %>% filter(STATEFP == 55) %>% st_transform(3735)

wi_sd        <- st_read("C:/Users/aryan/OneDrive - American Bankers Association/Documents/GitHub/Wisconsin_Tax/data/shapefiles/Wisconsin_School_Districts_-5132457395192808409/WI_School_Districts.shp") |> st_transform(3735)

# Wisconsin land polygon (counties are shoreline-clipped, so their union excludes Lake
# Erie). Clip the other jurisdiction layers to it so the lake doesn't render.
wi_land        <- sf::st_union(sf::st_make_valid(wi_county))
wi_cities_l    <- clip_to_land(wi_city, wi_land)
wi_townships_l <- clip_to_land(wi_township, wi_land)
wi_villages_l  <- clip_to_land(wi_village, wi_land)
wi_sd_l        <- clip_to_land(wi_sd, wi_land)
n_cities <- nrow(wi_city); n_twp <- nrow(wi_township); n_sd <- nrow(wi_sd)
n_villages <- nrow(wi_village)

# School-district IRN -> TIGER GEOID crosswalk (used by the SD maps). This is the
# VALIDATED crosswalk from 1i-sd-geoid-crosswalk.py: it keeps a raw NCES id only
# when it is a real Ohio TIGER GEOID (a handful of raw rows carry out-of-state
# placeholder ids), then falls back to a name+county match. 606/614 ODT districts
# resolve (vs 18 unmatched under the raw join); the residual ~5 are same-named
# districts logged in 05_output/audit/sd_geoid_unmatched.csv.
xwalk <- readr::read_csv(here("04_data-clean/crosswalks/ohio_irn_to_tiger_geoid.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(irn = as.character(irn), geoid = as.character(geoid)) |>
  filter(!is.na(geoid))
```

This document builds the descriptive baseline that the replacement-scenario model (`02_code/scenarios/`, Part II) perturbs when estimating the consequences of abolishing Ohio's **real property tax**. We organize it around four questions — *who* taxes, *what* they may levy, *what* they collect, and *what* they spend — then turn to how the ACS/PUMS household data converts those fiscal totals into a household-incidence baseline, for both the property tax and the income tax. The recurring finding: property tax is a **local, school-centred, real-property** instrument distributed unevenly across Ohio, so a statewide replacement is never a clean swap.

# (i) Who are the taxing authorities?

Ohio property tax is levied not by one government but by a stack of overlapping ones — counties, municipalities (cities and villages), townships, and school districts, plus special districts (libraries, parks, transit). A single parcel typically pays into several at once. That overlap is why "abolish the property tax" is hundreds of simultaneous fiscal events, not one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jurisdictions
#| fig-cap: "Ohio's four overlapping kinds of property-taxing authority (Lake Erie removed)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
base_map <- function(layer, title)
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = layer, fill = swank_palette[1], color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_sf(data = wi_land, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
    labs(title = title) + theme_swank_map(base_size = 11)

p_jur <- (base_map(wi_county, "Counties") | base_map(wi_cities_l, paste(n_cities, "Municipalities"))) /
         base_map(wi_villages_l, paste(n_villages, "Villages")) | (base_map(wi_townships_l, paste(n_twp, "Townships")) | base_map(wi_sd_l, paste(n_sd, "School districts"))) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Four overlapping kinds of taxing authority levy Ohio's property tax",
    subtitle = "Each parcel sits inside a county, a municipality or township, and a school district at once",
    caption = "Source: Census TIGER (counties, school districts) + ODOT/OGRIP (Ohio_City_Boundaries.shp, Ohio_Township_Boundaries.shp).",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))
  )
p_jur
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig04_jurisdictions_small_multiples.png"),
       p_jur, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

School districts and townships tile the whole state; municipalities are islands of denser settlement. The model carries all four levels because replacement revenue routed to one level does not automatically reach the level that lost it — the heart of the Layer-2 redistribution problem.

# (ii) What may each authority levy — and at what rates?

Not every government can levy every tax. This is the single most useful fact for reasoning about replacement: when the property tax disappears, only certain levels have other instruments to fall back on, and the property tax is the *only* broad tax a township or special district has at all.

```{r}
#| label: prep-sd-income-count
# Hoisted here (ahead of the section-iii map that otherwise builds it first)
# so the "how many districts levy a school income tax" figure quoted in
# this section and in the open item further below is a live count, not a
# hand-typed one -- same construction the fig-sd-income chunk in section
# iii uses (ODT Table SD-2, FY2026 Q4); that chunk reuses this object
# rather than re-deriving it.
sd2_m <- read_excel(raw("Local Tax/School_Income_Tax/sd2q4fy26.xlsx"),
                    sheet = "SD2Q4_FY26", col_names = FALSE)
sd_income <- tibble(
  irn = as.character(sd2_m[[4]]),                              # col 4 = IRN
  q1 = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sd2_m[[9]])),  q2 = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sd2_m[[10]])),
  q3 = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sd2_m[[11]])), q4 = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sd2_m[[12]]))  # cols 9-12 = quarters
) |>
  filter(!is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(irn)))) |>
  mutate(sd_income = rowSums(across(c(q1, q2, q3, q4)), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(irn, sd_income)
n_sd_income_positive <- sum(sd_income$sd_income > 0)
```

| Authority | Property tax | Sales / use tax | Income tax | Other notable |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| **State of Wisconsin** | — | **✓** 5.0% | **✓** 3.50–7.65% individual | corporate franchise/income, motor fuel, alcohol/tobacco and other excises |
| **County** | **✓** | **✓** generally 0.5%; Milwaukee Co. 0.9% | — | qualifying counties may impose premier resort area tax |
| **City** | **✓** | Limited[^wi-muni-sales] | — | municipal room tax; TIF; special charges/fees |
| **Village** | **✓** | Limited[^wi-muni-sales] | — | municipal room tax; TIF; special charges/fees |
| **Town** | **✓** | Limited[^wi-muni-sales] | — | municipal room tax; TIF; special charges/fees |
| **School district** | **✓** | — | — | referendum-approved levy/debt authority |
| **Technical college district** | **✓** | — | — | — |
| **Special district** (sanitary, sewerage, lake, etc.) | **✓** in many cases | Limited[^wi-special-sales] | — | special assessments / charges |

[^wi-muni-sales]: Municipal sales taxation is very limited in Wisconsin. The **City of Milwaukee** is the only municipality with a general city sales/use tax, at 2%. Qualifying cities, villages, and towns may instead impose a **Premier Resort Area Tax** on specified taxable sales. This authority applies only to designated resort municipalities and is not general municipal sales-tax authority.

[^wi-special-sales]: Special-district sales taxes are unusual rather than a general feature of Wisconsin local taxation. Milwaukee-area local exposition taxes are a notable example and apply to selected activities such as lodging, food and beverages, and rental cars.

: Which Ohio governments may levy which broad taxes

**Notes.** ^†^ *Selective excises* are narrow taxes on specific goods (cigarette, alcohol, motor fuel, etc.) — distinct from the broad **sales / use tax** on general retail, which is the only thing meant by "sales tax" in this column. ^‡^ *Permissive* sales tax: a **county** may levy up to **1.5%**, and a transit authority additional increments; combined local rates reach \~2.25%. ^§^ Townships have **no income-tax authority of their own**. They can share in an income tax only through a **JEDD** (Joint Economic Development District) — a contract with a municipality that imposes the *municipality's* income tax inside a defined zone. **SD** = school district. The **state income tax** is a flat 2.75%, but only on Ohio taxable income **above ≈ \$26,050** — income at or below that threshold owes no state income tax (so the first \~\$26k of taxable income is effectively exempt).

Three things to read off @tbl-authority. First, **townships and special districts have only the property tax** — abolition leaves them with no broad local instrument at all. Second, **counties can reach a sales tax but not an income tax**; municipalities the reverse. Third, **schools have two tools** — property tax and a voted income tax — but rely overwhelmingly on the first (section iii). About `r n_sd_income_positive` (FY2026 SD-2) school districts and 600+ municipalities levy income taxes.

The *rates* themselves vary enormously across space. The clearest example is the residential (Class I) school property-tax rate, which is what a homeowner actually pays per dollar of value after HB 920:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sd-rate
#| fig-cap: "Class I (residential/agricultural) effective school property-tax millage, TY2025, with 20-mill-floor districts outlined in red (Lake Erie removed)."
# Column positions mirror 06_writing/webpage/build_authority_maps.py's
# section D (same source file): col 7 = Total Class I effective rate, col 29
# = "Class I 20-mill Floor Rate". The at_floor rule (|floor rate - 20| <=
# 0.01) and the red-outline convention are copied from that builder so this
# static map and the interactive authority map read identically.
sd_rates <- read_odt(raw("Local Tax/Property_Tax_Rates/2025-sd-rates.xlsx"),
                     sheet = "School2025", header_token = "Home County Name") |>
  select(irn = 4, class1_rate = 7, floor_c1 = 29) |>
  mutate(irn = as.character(irn),
         class1_rate = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(class1_rate)),
         floor_c1    = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(floor_c1)),
         at_floor    = !is.na(floor_c1) & abs(floor_c1 - 20) <= 0.01)

n_sd_rated <- sum(!is.na(sd_rates$floor_c1))
n_sd_floor <- sum(sd_rates$at_floor, na.rm = TRUE)

sd_rate_map <- oh_sd_l |>
  left_join(xwalk, by = c("GEOID" = "geoid")) |>
  left_join(sd_rates, by = "irn")

p_fig8 <- ggplot(sd_rate_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = class1_rate), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(sd_rate_map, at_floor),
          aes(color = "At the 20-mill floor"), fill = NA, linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_sf(data = oh_land, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(name = "Class I effective mills", labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("At the 20-mill floor" = "#c0392b"), name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8))) +
  labs(title = "Residential school property-tax rates vary widely across districts",
       subtitle = "Class I (residential/agricultural) effective millage by school district (TY2025)",
       caption = paste0("Source: ODT 2025 SD rates (2025-sd-rates.xlsx) + validated IRN-GEOID crosswalk + TIGER SD shapefile.\n",
                        "Floor status from the Class I 20-mill Floor Rate column; outlines match the interactive authority map.")) +
  theme_swank_map()
p_fig8
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig08_school_district_class1_rate_2025.png"),
       p_fig8, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Districts at the HB 920 **20-mill floor** are the map's second story, and the bigger one: `r n_sd_floor` of the `r n_sd_rated` rated districts (`r scales::percent(n_sd_floor / n_sd_rated, accuracy = 1)`) sit at the floor — outlined in red above, matching the interactive authority map's convention. A floor district's Class I current-expense millage cannot be reduced further by HB 920 reduction factors, so its revenue *does* grow with reassessment, unlike districts above the floor, whose effective rate falls as values rise. Floor and non-floor districts would therefore lose very different amounts under any statewide replacement — the entry point to the Layer-3 school-finance analysis.

> **Note (mostly resolved).** The IRN→GEOID match is now the *validated* crosswalk (`1i-sd-geoid-crosswalk.py`): 606 of 614 ODT districts attach a rate, up from the 18 left grey under the raw join. The residual \~5 grey districts are same-named districts (e.g. Lakota/Madison/Perry/Green Local) whose county tie-break didn't land, plus defunct/merged IRNs — all listed in `05_output/audit/sd_geoid_unmatched.csv`. **Alex:** if we publish this map, hand-resolve those last few GEOIDs and note any taxable value they represent.

# (iii) What does each level collect?

## The macro picture

```{r}
#| label: fig-collections-stacked
#| fig-cap: "Ohio state and local tax collections by type, stacked by level (mixed vintages)."
collections <- readr::read_csv(
  here("04_data-clean/intermediate/collections_by_type.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(collections_b = collections_usd / 1e9)

# Real property and public-utility tangible property totals, read once here
# and inlined everywhere this document quotes them (never hand-typed).
real_prop_b <- collections$collections_b[collections$tax_type == "Property tax (real, net charged)"]
put_b       <- collections$collections_b[collections$tax_type == "Public utility tangible property tax"]

tax_cols <- c(
  "Property tax (real, net charged)"      = "#1F3864",
  "Public utility tangible property tax"  = "#8496B0",  # distinct instrument, kept visually adjacent
  "Municipal income tax"         = "#2E7D32",
  "Sales tax (county & transit)" = "#9CC3E5",
  "School district income tax"   = "#A9D18E",
  # "Public library fund"          = "#BFBFBF",
  "Sales & use tax"              = "#5B9BD5",
  "Individual income tax"        = "#70AD47",
  "Commercial Activity Tax"      = "#ED7D31",
  "Motor fuel tax"               = "#A6611A",
  "Other taxes (smaller)"  = "#7F7F7F"
)
ord <- collections |> count(tax_type, wt = collections_b, sort = TRUE) |> pull(tax_type)
stack_df <- collections |> mutate(tax_type = factor(tax_type, levels = rev(ord)))

p_fig3 <- ggplot(stack_df, aes(level, collections_b, fill = tax_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(collections_b >= 2,
          paste0(str_wrap(tax_type, 16), "\n$", formatC(collections_b, 1, format = "f"), "B"), "")),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 2.6, lineheight = 0.85,
    color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tax_cols, breaks = ord, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(suffix = "B"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "Property tax dominates local revenue; sales & income dominate the state",
       subtitle = "Ohio state & local tax collections by type (mixed vintages: FY2025 / TY2024 / CY2024 / CY2025 / TY2025)",
       x = NULL, y = "Collections",
       caption = "Source: ODT Tax Data Series") +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.text = element_text(size = 8), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
p_fig3
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig03_collections_state_local_stacked.png"),
       p_fig3, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Local **real** property tax (`r dollar(real_prop_b, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` net charged, TY2025 — plus a further `r dollar(put_b, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` of public-utility *tangible* property tax, a legally distinct instrument the amendment does not touch) is the single largest tax in the state — larger than the state sales tax or income tax. That `r dollar(real_prop_b, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` is the magnitude of the hole, and it is *local*. And it is concentrated on schools:

```{r}
#| label: fig-jurisdiction-shares
#| fig-cap: "Share of Ohio property-tax collections by jurisdiction type (Government Finance Database, 2022)."
jur <- read_parquet(here("03_data-raw/external/govt_finance_database/midwest_2005_present.parquet"),
                    col_select = all_of(c("state_name", "year", "govt_type_label", "Property_Tax"))) |>
  filter(state_name == "Ohio", year == 2022, govt_type_label != "State") |>
  group_by(govt_type_label) |>
  summarise(ptax = sum(Property_Tax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct = round(ptax / sum(ptax) * 100, 1)) |>
  arrange(pct) |>
  mutate(govt_type_label = factor(govt_type_label, levels = govt_type_label),
         highlight = as.character(govt_type_label) == "School District")

p_fig12 <- ggplot(jur, aes(pct, govt_type_label, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6, color = "#404040") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = swank_palette[2], `FALSE` = "#BFBFBF"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)), limits = c(0, 75)) +
  labs(title = "School districts collect two-thirds of Ohio's property tax",
       subtitle = "Property tax collected by jurisdiction type — Government Finance Database, Ohio 2022",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Government Finance Database (Census of Governments), Ohio 2022. Reconcile to ODT property-tax tables before publishing.") +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_fig12
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig12_property_tax_by_jurisdiction.png"),
       p_fig12, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

<!-- This is now **computed from the Government Finance Database**, not lifted from the deck: school districts collect \~65% of Ohio property tax, counties \~17%, townships \~7%, municipalities \~6%, special districts \~4% (JVSDs fall inside "School District" here). The numbers sit close to Alex's deck figures; the publishable version still reconciles to ODT's property-tax tables, which are the statutory source of record. -->

Confirming against the **ODT property-tax Tax Data Series** (taxes charged by *type of taxing subdivision*) — the source of record, compiled from county-auditor abstracts — reveals close figures using both 2022 and 2025 data. One definitional difference to hold in mind when comparing the two: the GFD chart above folds Joint Vocational School Districts (JVSDs) into "School District," while the ODT-based charts below break JVSDs out as their own category (a few percent of the total) — so "close figures" means close *after* accounting for that JVSD split, not an exact like-for-like match.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jurisdiction-shares-odt-2022
#| fig-cap: "Allocated property tax levies by jurisdiction type — ODT Tax Data Series, Ohio 2022."
# ---- Property tax by jurisdiction type: ODT tax district allocation ---------
# Levy allocation itself (taxing-district levy split across overlapping
# political units by each unit's share of the district's gross tax rate) now
# lives in 02_code/1l-levy-allocation.R -- this chunk only aggregates its output
# to jurisdiction-type shares and plots. Promoted here to kill a copy-paste
# bug: this chunk and the 2025 chunk below used to be two ~115-line hand-
# duplicated blocks (see 09_quality_reports/plans/2026-07-13_phase3-model-
# descriptives.md, Phase 3C). odt() (identical to raw(), defined in setup)
# is used by later chunks in this document, not this one.

jur_2022 <- read_csv(here("04_data-clean/intermediate/levy_allocation_2022.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(jurisdiction_type), !is.na(allocated_levy)) |>
  group_by(jurisdiction_type) |>
  summarise(ptax = sum(allocated_levy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct = round(ptax / sum(ptax, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1)) |>
  arrange(pct) |>
  mutate(jurisdiction_type = factor(jurisdiction_type, levels = jurisdiction_type),
        highlight = jurisdiction_type == "School District")

p_fig12b_22 <- ggplot(jur_2022, aes(pct, jurisdiction_type, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6, color = "#404040") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = swank_palette[2], `FALSE` = "#BFBFBF"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)), limits = c(0, 75)) +
  labs(title = "School districts collect the largest share of Ohio property taxes",
       subtitle = "Allocated property tax levies by jurisdiction type — ODT Tax Data Series, Ohio 2022",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: ODT Tax Data Series, RPUAbs22 and rates22, via 02_code/1l-levy-allocation.R. Taxing-district levies allocated by each political unit's share of the gross tax rate.") +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_fig12b_22
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig12_property_tax_by_jurisdiction_odt_2022.png"),
       p_fig12b_22, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-jurisdiction-shares-odt-2025
#| fig-cap: "Allocated property tax levies by jurisdiction type — ODT Tax Data Series, Ohio 2025."
jur_2025 <- read_csv(here("04_data-clean/intermediate/levy_allocation_2025.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(jurisdiction_type), !is.na(allocated_levy)) |>
  group_by(jurisdiction_type) |>
  summarise(ptax = sum(allocated_levy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct = round(ptax / sum(ptax, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1)) |>
  arrange(pct) |>
  mutate(jurisdiction_type = factor(jurisdiction_type, levels = jurisdiction_type),
        highlight = jurisdiction_type == "School District")

p_fig12b_25 <- ggplot(jur_2025, aes(pct, jurisdiction_type, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6, color = "#404040") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = swank_palette[2], `FALSE` = "#BFBFBF"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)), limits = c(0, 75)) +
  labs(title = "School districts collect the largest share of Ohio property taxes",
       subtitle = "Allocated property tax levies by jurisdiction type — ODT Tax Data Series, Ohio 2025",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: ODT Tax Data Series") +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_fig12b_25
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig12_property_tax_by_jurisdiction_odt_2025.png"),
       p_fig12b_25, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

How dependent are schools on the property tax specifically? Of the **own-source (local) revenue** a district raises itself — setting aside state and federal aid — property tax is the overwhelming majority: districts levy the voted school income tax in only a minority of cases (the SD income-tax map further below in this section), so for most districts property tax *is* own-source revenue.

The precise own-source share is not yet computed from a reconciled district-finance source and is flagged here as an open item rather than asserted with false precision — see the note below and next-steps item 2. Two related, already-computed figures bound it from different directions: school districts collect the largest share of statewide property tax among jurisdiction types (the fig12 jurisdiction-type shares, above), and school districts are one of the two most property-tax-reliant levels of government by *total* revenue (§iv below) — a lower bound on the own-source share, since state and federal aid dilute the total-revenue denominator but not the own-source one.

> **Open item.** A June 2026 planning slide measured a related but different thing — property tax as a share of school *tax* revenue (property vs income tax) — which this document does not yet reproduce: the GFD's per-district school income-tax figure is unreliable (it flags \~446 districts with an income tax vs the `r n_sd_income_positive` that actually levy one, FY2026 SD-2). Building the property-vs-income version requires joining the ODT school-income-tax table (`sd2…`, the authoritative `r n_sd_income_positive` districts) to per-district property tax, or pulling **ODE&W** district-finance data (`03_data-raw/external/odew/`) for the full revenue-by-source breakdown.

## Collections over time (2005–2023)

Everything above is a single-year cross-section. The Government Finance Database (GFD) covers Ohio annually back to 2005 (full-coverage census years 2007/2012/2017/2022, an annual-survey sample in between), so we can ask whether property tax's role has been shrinking or growing relative to the other major instruments — directly relevant to the HB 920 erosion story.

```{r}
#| label: fig-collections-trend
#| fig-cap: "Ohio state + local tax collections by major instrument, 2005–2023 (nominal $, GFD)."
gfd_trend <- read_parquet(
  here("03_data-raw/external/govt_finance_database/midwest_2005_present.parquet"),
  col_select = all_of(c("state_name", "year", "Property_Tax", "Total_Gen_Sales_Tax", "Individual_Income_Tax", "Total_Taxes"))
) |>
  filter(state_name == "Ohio") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    `Property tax` = sum(Property_Tax, na.rm = TRUE) * 1000,
    `General sales tax` = sum(Total_Gen_Sales_Tax, na.rm = TRUE) * 1000,
    `Individual income tax` = sum(Individual_Income_Tax, na.rm = TRUE) * 1000,
    total_taxes = sum(Total_Taxes, na.rm = TRUE) * 1000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

trend_long <- gfd_trend |>
  select(-total_taxes) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "tax_type", values_to = "collections") |>
  mutate(collections_b = collections / 1e9)

p_trend <- ggplot(trend_long, aes(year, collections_b, color = tax_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = swank_palette[1:3], name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2005, 2023, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(suffix = "B"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  labs(title = "All three major Ohio taxes grew together; property tax never fell behind",
       subtitle = "State + local collections by instrument, all Ohio governments summed, 2005-2023 (nominal dollars)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Government Finance Database (Pierson, Hand & Thompson 2015), Ohio all-government sums. Nominal dollars, not inflation-adjusted -- a real (CPI-deflated) version is a next step. Non-census years (all but 2007/2012/2017/2022) are the Census Annual Survey sample, not a full count.") +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
p_trend
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig28_collections_trend_2005_2023.png"),
       p_trend, width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-property-share-trend
#| fig-cap: "Property tax's share of total Ohio state + local tax revenue, 2005–2023."
share_trend <- gfd_trend |>
  mutate(property_share = `Property tax` / total_taxes)
mean_share <- mean(share_trend$property_share, na.rm = TRUE)
range_share <- range(share_trend$property_share, na.rm = TRUE)

p_share_trend <- ggplot(share_trend, aes(year, property_share)) +
  geom_line(color = swank_palette[1], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = swank_palette[1], size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_share, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2005, 2023, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Property tax's share of total Ohio tax revenue has stayed remarkably flat",
       subtitle = "Property tax ÷ total state + local tax collections, all governments, 2005-2023",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = paste0("Source: Government Finance Database, Ohio all-government sums. Dashed line = 2005-2023 average (",
                        percent(mean_share, accuracy = 1), "). Range across all 19 years: ",
                        percent(range_share[1], accuracy = 1), "-", percent(range_share[2], accuracy = 1),
                        " -- no secular decline despite HB 920 reduction factors; new construction and reappraisal growth",
                        " have offset the millage erosion in the aggregate.")) +
  theme_swank() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
p_share_trend
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig29_property_tax_share_trend_2005_2023.png"),
       p_share_trend, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

The headline is a small surprise: property tax's **share** of total Ohio state-and-local tax revenue has held close to **`r percent(mean_share, accuracy = 1)`** every year since 2005 (range across all 19 years: `r percent(range_share[1], accuracy = 1)`–`r percent(range_share[2], accuracy = 1)`), with no visible secular decline — despite HB 920's reduction-factor mechanism, which is specifically designed to hold *effective rates* down as values rise. That is consistent with the standard HB 920 story once you separate rate from revenue: reduction factors cap the *rate* increase from reappraisal, but new construction (added to the tax base at the *full*, un-reduced rate) and voted levies still let aggregate collections grow roughly in step with the other major taxes. This is a state-level aggregate, not a claim about any one district — individual districts with little new construction can and do see real erosion, which is exactly the Layer-3 school-finance question. All figures here are **nominal dollars**; a CPI-deflated (real) version is flagged as a next step rather than estimated with a hand-typed inflation series. Two caveats on the series above it. First, **"Individual income tax" and "General sales tax" are state *and* local combined** (Census T40/T09 categories summed across every Ohio government) — a different, larger aggregate than the `r dollar(collections$collections_b[collections$tax_type == "Individual income tax"], accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` *state-only* individual income tax figure (TY2024, ODT Table Y-1) used in this document's income-tax baseline section below, so don't compare the two directly. Second, this GFD-derived trend has not yet been reconciled to the ODT Tax Data Series (the source of record per the project's source hierarchy) the way the single-year collections figures above it have been — treat the *trend* (flat, no erosion) as more load-bearing than any single year's *level* until that reconciliation is logged in `05_output/audit/audit_log.xlsx`.

## The geography of collections

Where the property tax is charged tracks property wealth and population:

```{r}
#| label: fig-county-property
#| fig-cap: "County net property tax charged, TY2025."
prop_county <- read_odt(raw("Local Tax/Property_Tax_Real_Property/pd23ty25.xlsx"),
                        sheet = "pd23ty25", header_token = "County") |>
  select(county = 1, prop_tax_thou = 12) |>
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county),
         prop_tax = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(prop_tax_thou)) * 1000) |>
  keep_oh_counties(county)

p_fig7 <- oh_counties |> left_join(prop_county, by = "county") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = prop_tax), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(name = "Net property tax charged", labels = label_usd_millions()) +
  labs(title = "Where Ohio's property tax is charged",
       subtitle = "Total net real + public-utility property taxes charged by county, tax year 2025",
       caption = "Source: ODT Table PD-23 (pd23ty25.xlsx), net of HB 920 reduction factors. Charged, not collected.") +
  theme_swank_map()
p_fig7
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig07_county_property_tax_2025.png"),
       p_fig7, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

The leading replacement candidate — the sales tax — is collected somewhere quite different. This is the **place-of-sale vs place-of-residence** distinction that is central to Layer 2: where a county *collects* sales tax is not where its residents *live* or where the lost property tax was *spent*.

```{r}
#| label: fig-county-sales
#| fig-cap: "County permissive sales/use tax collected, CY2025 (place of sale; county share only)."
# keep_oh_counties() keeps the 88 county rows and DROPS the transit-authority rows,
# so this map is the COUNTY permissive piece only (~$2.97B). The transit-authority
# permissive piece (~$0.98B, e.g. COTA/GCRTA/SARTA) is excluded; with it the S-1
# CY2025 grand total is ~$3.95B. The macro collections table (fig 2-3) instead uses
# the S-2 FY2025 permissive total (~$3.67B) — a different table, vintage, and
# coverage. Reconcile before publishing a single statewide local-sales number.
sales_use <- read_odt(raw("Local Tax/SU_Permissive_Tax/s1cy25.xlsx"),
                      sheet = "Summary", header_token = "County") |>
  keep_oh_counties(county) |>
  transmute(county, collections = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(cy_2025_total)))

p_fig6 <- oh_counties |> left_join(sales_use, by = "county") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = collections), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(name = "CY2025 collections", labels = label_usd_millions()) +
  labs(title = "Sales-tax collections concentrate where the selling happens",
       subtitle = "County permissive sales/use tax collected, calendar year 2025 (county share; transit excluded)",
       caption = "Source: ODT Table S-1 (s1cy25.xlsx, Summary), 88 county rows only — transit-authority permissive (~$1.0B) excluded. PLACE OF SALE, not residence or burden.") +
  theme_swank_map()
p_fig6
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig06_county_sales_use_tax_2025.png"),
       p_fig6, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Municipal income tax — the second-largest local tax — is mostly levied where people *work*, adding yet another geography to the mismatch story. One caveat to read the map with: LG-11 reports each municipality under a single **home county**, so a city that straddles county lines (Columbus spans Franklin, Delaware, and Fairfield) has its *entire* collection booked to that one county. This is therefore a municipality-reported-county map, not a true workplace apportionment:

```{r}
#| label: fig-municipal-income
#| fig-cap: "Net municipal income-tax collections by municipality-reported county, CY2024."
lg11_m  <- read_excel(raw("Local Tax/Municipal_Income_Tax/lg11cy24.xlsx"),
                      sheet = "LG11CY24", col_names = FALSE)
muni_inc <- tibble(county   = as.character(lg11_m[[4]]),               # col 4 = County
                   net_coll = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(lg11_m[[6]]))) |>  # col 6 = Net Collections
  keep_oh_counties(county) |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(muni_income = sum(net_coll, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

p_fig13 <- oh_counties |> left_join(muni_inc, by = "county") |>
  mutate(muni_income = tidyr::replace_na(muni_income, 0)) |>   # Vinton has no reporting municipality -> $0, not grey
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = muni_income), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(option = "rocket", name = "Municipal income tax", labels = label_usd_millions()) +
  labs(title = "Municipal income tax is collected where the jobs are",
       subtitle = "Net municipal income-tax collections by municipality-reported county, calendar year 2024",
       caption = "Source: ODT Table LG-11 (lg11cy24.xlsx), summed to each municipality's reported home county (cross-county cities booked to one county). $0 = no reporting municipality.") +
  theme_swank_map()
p_fig13
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig13_municipal_income_by_county.png"),
       p_fig13, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

The property-tax, sales-tax, and municipal-income maps above look alike because all three taxes scale with population. To see whether they are actually paid in *different* places, we map each county's **share of the statewide total** for property tax minus its share of statewide (sales + municipal income). That strips out the size gap and exposes the divergence:

```{r}
#| label: fig-tax-mismatch
#| fig-cap: "Where property tax is paid vs where sales + municipal income are collected (share-of-statewide difference, ppt)."
mismatch <- prop_county |>
  select(county, prop_tax) |>
  left_join(select(sales_use, county, sales = collections), by = "county") |>
  left_join(muni_inc, by = "county") |>
  mutate(across(c(prop_tax, sales, muni_income), ~ tidyr::replace_na(.x, 0)),
         prop_sh = prop_tax / sum(prop_tax),
         alt_sh  = (sales + muni_income) / sum(sales + muni_income),
         diff_pp = (prop_sh - alt_sh) * 100)

p_mismatch <- oh_counties |> left_join(mismatch, by = "county") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = diff_pp), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_swank_div(name = "Property share − (sales+income) share, ppt") +
  labs(title = "Property tax and its replacements are paid in different places",
       subtitle = "County share of statewide property tax minus its share of statewide (sales + municipal income)",
       caption = paste("Source: ODT PD-23 / S-1 / LG-11. Green = over-weight in PROPERTY (residential/suburban);",
                       "purple = over-weight in SALES+INCOME (retail/job hubs). Shares normalise the size gap. Illustrative.")) +
  theme_swank_map()
p_mismatch
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig18_tax_place_mismatch.png"),
       p_mismatch, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Green counties contribute more to the *property* base than to the *sales+income* base — the residential and suburban places whose households would bear a replacement collected elsewhere; purple counties are the retail and employment hubs that collect sales and municipal income out of proportion to their property tax. This is the Layer-2 redistribution problem in one frame. It pools two different bases, so treat it as illustrative, not a settled estimate.

Schools' *other* tool — the voted income tax — is used by only a minority of districts, mostly rural and exurban ones, and raises far less than their property tax (`r dollar(collections$collections_b[collections$tax_type == "School district income tax"], accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` statewide per the Table SD-2-based collections total, vs `r dollar(real_prop_b, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "B")` real property; the SD-2 file's own direct sum across all districts, `r dollar(sum(sd_income$sd_income, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, accuracy = 0.001, suffix = "B")`, runs slightly higher — a small, unreconciled discrepancy between the two ways of totaling the same table). Grey districts levy no income tax at all:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sd-income
#| fig-cap: "Annual school-district income-tax distributions by district, FY2026 (grey = no income tax; Lake Erie removed)."
# sd_income (all districts, incl. $0) was hoisted to the prep-sd-income-count
# chunk in section (ii) above so a live district count is available before
# this chunk runs; reused here rather than re-derived.
p_sdinc <- oh_sd_l |>
  left_join(xwalk, by = c("GEOID" = "geoid")) |>
  left_join(sd_income, by = "irn") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = sd_income), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = oh_land, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(option = "rocket", name = "Annual SD income tax", labels = label_usd_millions()) +
  labs(title = "Only a minority of school districts levy an income tax",
       subtitle = "Annual school-district income-tax distributions by district, FY2026 (grey = no income tax)",
       caption = "Source: ODT Table SD-2 (sd2q4fy26.xlsx) + validated IRN-GEOID crosswalk + TIGER unified SD shapefile.") +
  theme_swank_map()
p_sdinc
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig14_school_district_income_tax_2026.png"),
       p_sdinc, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Finally, who *bears* the property tax locally depends on the class composition of each county's base — residential/agricultural (Class I) vs commercial, industrial, and mineral (Class II; public-utility tangible property is the separate PUT instrument, not Class II real property).

Based on share of taxable value:

```{r}
#| label: fig-residential-share
#| fig-cap: "Residential & agricultural share of taxable real-property value by county, TY2024."
pd31 <- read_odt(raw("State Tax/Property_Tax/pd31cy24.xlsx"), header_token = "County") |>
  select(county = 1, residential_value = 2, total_value = 17) |>
  mutate(across(c(residential_value, total_value), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x)))) |>
  keep_oh_counties(county) |>
  mutate(residential_share = residential_value / total_value)

p_fig10 <- oh_counties |> left_join(pd31, by = "county") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residential_share), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_swank_seq(name = "Residential share", labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "How much of each county's tax base is residential",
       subtitle = "Residential & agricultural share of taxable real-property value, tax year 2024",
       caption = "Source: ODT Table PD-31 (pd31cy24.xlsx). Share of VALUE (proxy for tax share; HB 920 class rates differ).") +
  theme_swank_map()
p_fig10
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig10_residential_share_value_2024.png"),
       p_fig10, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Based on share of taxes levied:

```{r}

# ---- Percent of each county's property tax levy from residential property --

property_tax_residential_share <- read_excel(
  odt("Local Tax/Property_Tax_Real_Property/rpuabs25.xlsx"),
  skip = 3,
  sheet = "RPUAbs25"
) |>
  filter(`Field Name` == "Current real and public utility taxes levied") |>

    residential_levy = as.numeric(residential_levy),

p_fig10_b <- oh_counties |>
  left_join(property_tax_residential_share, by = "county") |>

  ) +

    subtitle = "Residential share of current real and public utility taxes levied, tax year 2025",

  ) +

p_fig10_b
```

# Explore: county collections (interactive)

The three county-level taxes above — property, sales, and municipal income — are easiest to compare side by side. Use the layer control to recolour the map by each tax; hover a county to read all three values at once.

```{r interactive-map}
#| column: page
cty_i <- oh_counties |>
  left_join(prop_county, by = "county") |>
  left_join(sales_use,   by = "county") |>
  left_join(muni_inc,    by = "county") |>
  st_transform(4326)

fmtM <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "n/a", paste0("$", formatC(x / 1e6, 1, format = "f"), "M"))
labs_html <- sprintf(
  "<b>%s County</b><br/>Property tax: %s<br/>Sales tax: %s<br/>Municipal income: %s",
  cty_i$county, fmtM(cty_i$prop_tax), fmtM(cty_i$collections), fmtM(cty_i$muni_income)
) |> lapply(htmltools::HTML)

pal_prop  <- colorNumeric("YlGnBu", cty_i$prop_tax,    na.color = "#eeeeee")
pal_sales <- colorNumeric("BuPu",   cty_i$collections, na.color = "#eeeeee")
pal_muni  <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", cty_i$muni_income, na.color = "#eeeeee")

leaflet(cty_i) |>
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.PositronNoLabels") |>
  addPolygons(group = "Property tax", fillColor = ~pal_prop(prop_tax), weight = 0.6,
              color = "white", fillOpacity = 0.85, label = labs_html,
              highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = "#333", bringToFront = TRUE)) |>
  addPolygons(group = "Sales tax", fillColor = ~pal_sales(collections), weight = 0.6,
              color = "white", fillOpacity = 0.85, label = labs_html) |>
  addPolygons(group = "Municipal income", fillColor = ~pal_muni(muni_income), weight = 0.6,
              color = "white", fillOpacity = 0.85, label = labs_html) |>
  addLayersControl(baseGroups = c("Property tax", "Sales tax", "Municipal income"),
                   options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)) |>
  addControl("Switch layers (top-right) to recolour; hover for all three taxes.",
             position = "topleft")
```

This is the same place-of-X point in interactive form: the county that lights up for sales tax is rarely the one that lights up for property tax, and the municipal income map (place of work) is different again. Holding that geography in mind is the whole reason Layer 2 is hard.

# (iv) What does each level spend?

Collections are only half the ledger. Using the Government Finance Database (Pierson, Hand & Thompson 2015; Ohio 2022, a Census year), we can see what each local level actually funds — and therefore what loses its revenue source under abolition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-expenditure
#| fig-cap: "What each local government spends on, Ohio 2022 (share of expenditure; total $B labelled)."
exp <- readr::read_csv(here("04_data-clean/processed/ohio_expenditure_by_jurisdiction_2022.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  group_by(govt_type) |>
  mutate(total_b = sum(expenditure_usd) / 1e9, share = expenditure_usd / sum(expenditure_usd)) |>
  ungroup()

gt_order  <- exp |> distinct(govt_type, total_b) |> arrange(desc(total_b)) |> pull(govt_type)
cat_order <- exp |> filter(category != "Other") |> group_by(category) |>
  summarise(s = sum(expenditure_usd), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(s) |> pull(category)
exp <- exp |> mutate(govt_type = factor(govt_type, levels = gt_order),
                     category  = factor(category, levels = c("Other", cat_order)))

)

p_exp <- ggplot(exp, aes(govt_type, share, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = distinct(exp, govt_type, total_b),
            aes(govt_type, 1.01, label = paste0("$", formatC(total_b, 1, format = "f"), "B")),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = 0, size = 3, fontface = "bold", color = "#404040") +
```
